> 比。吉。原筮，元永貞，無咎。

比 looks like the friendliest word in the book. Two people, side by side.

The 彖 does not let it stay friendly.

## 比 is 反從

說文: 比，密也。二人為從，反從為比.

從 is two people following one another, walking in sequence. 比 is that pair turned around — standing side by side, joined.

So the original sense is closeness, adjacency, being joined. The oracle-bone form is two figures leaning shoulder to shoulder.

And then the 彖 glosses: 比，輔也，下順從也 — support, and the lower following the upper.

Which is the whole argument of the hexagram. 比 in the 易 is not the friendship of equals. It is the bond of allegiance: the lower attaching to the upper.

That is not a smaller thing than friendship. It is a different thing, and it has different failure modes — the failure of 比 is not distance, it is attaching to the wrong support.

## 原筮: examine, then examine again

原，再也 (孔穎達) — divining a second time before deciding. Or 推原其本 — tracing back to the source.

The two do not conflict: the reason for divining again is to trace the source again.

擇主之前，先審，再审. Before you attach, look; then look again. The hexagram puts the double examination into the judgement line, which means it belongs to the condition of the hexagram and not to the advice at the end.

## 缶: a clay pot

有孚盈缶.

缶 is earthenware, the plain vessel for wine and water (說文 缶，瓦器，所以盛酒漿).

盈 is full — and the precision is in that word. Full is not much. Full is a plain condition: what is in it is in it, and there is no room for anything else.

So 有孚盈缶 is trustworthiness described as a full jar: unornamented, and complete enough that it cannot hold a second thing.

## 三驅: three sides enclosed, one left open

九五 顯比，王用三驅，失前禽.

The archaic hunting rite: surround on three sides and leave one open.

So the king's 比 is 顯 — open, not a private arrangement — and its shape is a hunt that deliberately lets the front animals go.

Come and you are received; leave and you are not chased. Which is the only way attaching can be voluntary, and the only way it stays 顯 rather than 黨.

## 後夫凶

The one who attaches last, after watching how it turns out, is 凶.

This is the hexagram's sharpest line, and it is not about punishment. By the time the outcome is visible, the thing being attached to is no longer what you attached to. The moment has gone; the joining is now a formality.

## 無首, and how it differs from 乾

上六 比之無首，凶.

Here 無首 means: no central and correct head to attach to, so people attach randomly, in factions.

This is the same phrase as 乾's 見群龍無首，吉 — and it is the easiest confusion in the book.

In 乾, no single head is the good condition: no one has become the standard the others are measured against.

In 比, no single head is the bad condition: there is nothing to attach to, so allegiance scatters.

Same characters, opposite judgements — because the subject differs. In 乾 the question is whether one has become the measure. In 比 the question is whether there is a support at all. 不可為典要 is not a slogan; it is this.

## A test

Take an allegiance you hold — to a person, an institution, a line of work. Ask what you attached to, and whether that is still the thing you are attached to. 比 fails quietly: the attachment stays and the support changes.
